# Governance

How Open Agent Rules changes, and what an implementer can rely on.

## Versions

A version is `<major>.<minor>`.

**Minor.** Adding an optional field, adding an enum member, or clarifying wording that does not
change what a conforming engine does. Every document valid under the previous minor stays
valid. A loader that supports the major accepts every minor of it.

**Major.** Removing or renaming a required field, changing the decision an existing valid
document produces, or narrowing an existing field's accepted values. A loader that does not
support a major **rejects the document and fails closed** — it never coerces, downgrades, or
guesses.

Version 1.1 is additive over 1.0: it adds `namespace`, `requires_facts`, and `profile`, closes
the unknown-field policy behind an `x-` allowance, and deprecates `code`. Every valid 1.0
document is a valid 1.1 document.

## The one-change rule

A proposal is accepted only as a **single change containing all three of**:

1. the specification clause,
2. the schema edit, and
3. at least one conformance fixture.

A change with prose but no fixture is rejected. This is the mechanism that keeps the corpus
honest: a build gate fails when a normative MUST clause has no fixture covering it, so a
requirement can never be added and quietly left uncheckable. The same gate is why the
exemption list carries a sentence of justification per entry rather than a blanket rule.

Adding an exemption is a signal to re-read the clause. Most clauses that seem unfixturable
turn out to be mis-specified.

## Clause identifiers

Clause identifiers are `OAR-<AREA>-<n>`. They are **append-only**: never renumbered, never
reused, never recycled with a different meaning. A requirement that is retired is marked
obsolete in place and keeps its identifier, so a citation made years earlier still resolves.

A build gate fails if an identifier that appeared in a released version is missing from the
current text.

## Compatibility classes

**Decision identifiers are agent-public.** The identifier a decision carries is the contract
with everything downstream: agents branch on it, tooling routes on it, dashboards group by it.
Message text is not — it may be reworded at any time, and software that branches on message
text is broken by design, not by the change that broke it.

Changing what an existing identifier *means* is therefore a major version change, exactly as
if a required field had been renamed. Retiring one is not: an identifier that stops being
produced simply stops appearing.

Two publishers may ship the same bare identifier. Rule identity is the pair
(`namespace`, `id`), so those rules coexist; the rendered identifier stays the bare `id`, which
is why publisher scoping did not break the class.

## Extensions

Fields prefixed `x-` are reserved for implementations. Another implementation **ignores** them
rather than rejecting the document, and an `x-` field never acquires normative meaning without
a specification change. Everything else the document model does not define is rejected — the
alternative is a typo that silently does nothing, which is how a guardrail becomes a
placebo.

Host-specific observations live under a namespace the host owns, written `<host>.<fact>`. A
rule that uses one is legal and is not portable, and the specification says so rather than
pretending otherwise.

## Naming conventions

**Rule identifiers** are `SCREAMING_SNAKE`, match `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*$`, equal the file stem when
rules are stored one per file, and are stable for the life of the rule. Never reuse one with a
different meaning.

**Publisher namespaces** are lowercase, dot-separated, reverse-DNS-ish — `acme.security`,
`globex.policy` — one per publishing organisation. Identity is (`namespace`, `id`); the
rendered identifier stays the bare `id`.

**Host fact namespaces** use the host's own short name as the prefix, and are reserved to the
host that publishes them.

**Extension fields** are `x-<vendor>-<name>`, so two implementations' extensions cannot
collide.

## Who decides

Painted Wolf maintains this specification.

## How to propose a change

Open an issue or a pull request on the standard repository describing the behaviour you want,
the clause it changes, and the fixture that would prove it. Quote the clause identifier — that
is what it is for.

Note that `spec/` and `site/` in the standard repository are a **generated mirror**. Pull
requests against them are closed; the change lands in the engine repository's `spec/oar/` tree
and the mirror follows. The issue tracker is the right place to argue about a clause either
way.
